content: Tar, also known as tobacco residue, refers to the resinous, partially combusted particulate matter generated during the burning of tobacco, cannabis, and other plant materials in the act of smoking. It is widely recognized as the most harmful component of habitual tobacco smoking. Over time, tar accumulates in the lungs of smokers, causing damage through a variety of biochemical and mechanical processes. Tar contains the majority of mutagenic and carcinogenic agents found in tobacco smoke, as identified by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) in 1986. For instance, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) present in tar are genotoxic, primarily through a process called epoxidation. There is a common misconception that the tar in cigarettes is the same as the tar used in road construction. To address this misunderstanding, cigarette companies in the United States often place the word tar in quotation marks when providing tar and nicotine ratings for their products, emphasizing that it is not the same as the material used for road surfaces. Occasionally, tar is referred to as an acronym for total aerosol residue, although this may actually be a backronym rather than its original intended meaning. In the European Union, regulations currently limit the tar yield of cigarettes to a maximum of 10 milligrams per cigarette.
